frames.narration: A user in the city centre asks for restaurants within 2 km. With no spatial index the API computes the distance to all 2,000 restaurants and keeps the 855 inside the circle.

An ordinary B-tree index on latitude narrows only one coordinate: rows within 2 km north or south. That band, 4 km tall, crosses the whole 16 km city, so 1,307 restaurants are still read for 855 results.

A geo index cuts the map into cells and files each restaurant under its cell key (a geohash prefix). With 2 km cells, the user's own cell holds 221 restaurants, but only 200 of the 855 answers: the user stands on a cell corner.

The fix for the edge problem: read the cell and its 8 neighbours. Cells at least as wide as the radius make the 3 x 3 block cover the whole circle. 1,207 candidates come back, and an exact distance check keeps all 855.

One cell size cannot suit both the dense centre and the sparse suburbs. A quadtree splits any square holding more than 16 restaurants into four. The centre search reads 149 small leaves and checks 1,038 restaurants; a suburb search checks only 77.

Couriers move. 3,000 couriers sending a position every 4 seconds is 750 updates per second. Each update overwrites the courier's single latest entry, moving it to a new cell when needed, in memory (for example Redis GEOADD) rather than in the main database.

At city scale the index is split into shards by cell, so a search reads one shard or two at a border. The centre cells are hot, holding most restaurants and most searches, so they are split into smaller cells on their own shards.
